Energetic? Lord, no. I don't think I've felt energetic since... well, I can't even remember. It feels like years. Honestly, most days it's exactly the opposite. It's like I'm walking through molasses. Getting off the couch just to go to the kitchen and pour a glass of water feels like this massive undertaking. I just sit there.

I've never had a time where I felt like I could just go and go and go without resting. ========== OUTPUT [patient] ==========
Lost interest? Yeah, I'd say so. I'd say I've lost interest in just about everything, honestly. It's funny you ask that, because I was just thinking the other day about how different my Sundays used to be. I used to have a whole routine, you know? A whole schedule. I used to really look forward to choir practice. I'm not the best singer in the world, mind you, but I liked being part of it, the harmony, all those voices coming together. And then after choir, there was bridge. We had a regular group, four of us, and we'd play for hours. We weren't playing for money or anything, just bragging rights, but it was... it was nice. It felt good to use my brain like that, strategizing, trying to figure out what cards the others were holding. 

And cooking, too. I used to love making this big pot of beans every Sunday. My grandmother's recipe, with the ham hock and the onions, letting it simmer all day so the whole apartment smelled like it. I'd make enough to last me half the week. I even used to do little repair jobs for folks around the building, you know? Fixing a leaky faucet, tightening up a loose cabinet hinge. I liked feeling useful. I liked working with my hands. 

But now? Now I don't do any of it. None of it. The choir director called a few times, left messages, but I just let the phone ring. I sit there on the couch and watch it ring, and I just tell myself there's no point in going. There's just no point. The bridge group probably found a replacement by now, and I haven't cooked those beans in months. The thought of chopping the onions, standing over the stove... it's just too much. I don't have it in me. And I certainly don't want to be going into anyone else's apartment to fix their cabinets when I know half of them are the ones whispering about me to the management. Why would I help them? But even if they weren't, I just... I don't care anymore. The things that used to bring me a little bit of joy, a little bit of satisfaction, they just feel empty now. It's like all the color drained out of them, and I'm just left sitting here in the gray, waiting for the day to be over. So, yes, I've lost interest. Completely.

Every time I open my front door, I hear a deadbolt click, or I see somebody's blinds twitching out of the corner of my eye. \n\nAnd they're not just watching, they're actually slipping notes about me to the management office. I've seen them sneaking around the hallways with these pieces of paper. I try to mind my own business, I keep my TV turned down low, I don't bother a single soul, but they are constantly reporting on me. \n\nAnd the thing that really drives me crazy—and I guess why I was told I needed to come talk to you—is that everybody keeps telling me it's just regular notices on the doors. The property manager, my family, they all try to brush it off and tell me, \"Oh, it's just flyers for pest control,\" or \"They're just taping up water shut-off notices.\" But I know what I'm looking at. I know they're writing things down about exactly when I leave for the store and when I come back, and it's just... it's exhausting, honestly, having to look over your shoulder every single time you just want to step outside to check the mail.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: Voices? No, no, it's not like that. I'm not... I don't hear things that aren't there, if that's what you're asking. I mean, I hear *people* talking, but they are real people. You know how these apartment buildings are, especially the older ones like mine. They must have built this place thirty, forty years ago, and they didn't put a lick of insulation between the drywall. \n\nSo, if somebody is out in the hallway, or lingering by the stairwell—which they do, constantly—I can hear them mumbling. I can hear them whispering to each other. I can't always make out every single word, but I know it's them coordinating their little shifts, talking about what I'm doing. But it's not voices in my head or anything like that. It's just the actual neighbors. The guy in 2B, or that woman who walks her dog at all hours. \n\nI hear the floorboards creaking under the cheap carpet out there. I hear the tape ripping when they stick those notes on the doors. I hear the deadbolts. I just sit in my living room, completely quiet, sometimes for hours with the TV on mute, and I just listen to it all. And you wouldn't believe the amount of rustling and whispering that goes on right outside my door if you really pay attention. So I hear all of that, yes, but not... not ghosts or imaginary voices, no. Just the people who won't leave me be.\n\nDoctor: Have you had the feeling that someone else is putting thoughts into your mind or controlling your thoughts?\n\nPatient: Controlling my thoughts? No, no, nothing like that. My thoughts are my own. I mean, they can watch me all they want out there, they can write down every little thing I do and slip their little notes around to the management, but they can't get inside my head. \n\nI've got a lot of time to think, you know, not working and just being stuck in that apartment most of the day. I do a whole lot of thinking. I sit there on the couch, TV muted like I said, and I just turn things over in my mind. I think about how things used to be before this whole complex went downhill, or I try to figure out the patterns of what the neighbors are doing. But nobody is putting those thoughts in there. It's just me. \n\nI've always had a strong mind, always knew my own mind, even back when I was younger. I might not have finished high school, but I'm not stupid, and I know the difference between my own thoughts and... well, whatever else. So if you're asking if they have some kind of way to beam things into my brain, or if they're pulling strings in my head like a puppet? No. They're just sneaky people out in the hallway. I have to use my own brain to try and stay one step ahead of them, honestly. It takes a lot of mental energy to keep track of it all, trying to piece together why they're so interested in me, but it's all my own doing. Nobody's controlling what's up here but me.\n\nDoctor: Have there been times when you felt unusually energetic and needed much less sleep than usual?\n\nPatient: Energetic? Lord, no. I don't think I've felt energetic since... well, I can't even remember. It feels like years. Honestly, most days it's exactly the opposite. It's like I'm walking through molasses. Getting off the couch just to go to the kitchen and pour a glass of water feels like this massive undertaking. I just sit there. \n\nAnd as for sleep... well, I sleep all the time, really. Or at least, I try to. I'll lay down in the afternoon because I'm just so completely drained, physically and mentally drained from just existing in that apartment and listening to the hallway. I'll pull the blanket up, even if it's two o'clock in the afternoon, and I'll just stay there. Sometimes I sleep, sometimes I just lay there staring at the ceiling fan because I don't have the energy to do anything else. \n\nI've never had a time where I felt like I could just go and go and go without resting. I know some people get like that, my brother used to be able to work a double shift and then go fishing, but not me. I need my sleep. And lately, it feels like no matter how much I sleep, I wake up just as tired. It's a heavy kind of tired, you know? Like it's settled right into my bones. So, no, definitely not unusually energetic. Not even a little bit. I'd give anything for just a fraction of some energy, just enough to maybe clean the kitchen counters, but it's just not there.\n\nDoctor: How long have you been feeling that your neighbors are watching you and reporting on you?\n\nPatient: Well, let me think on that. It’s... it hasn't been forever, but when you're sitting in it every single day, it sure feels like a lifetime. If I had to put a strict timeline on it, I’d say it’s been about a year and a month now. Yeah, right around thirteen months. \n\nI know that because it was exactly when the building got bought out and they brought in that new management company for the front office. Before that, nobody cared what you did. You kept to yourself, they kept to themselves. But then this new office staff comes in, and suddenly there are all these new rules, new notices taped to everyone's doors every other week. And that’s exactly when I started noticing the neighbors acting strange. It was like the office put them up to it, you know? Like they told them to keep an eye on the older guy who's home all day. \n\nI remember it was a year and a month ago when I first caught that guy in 2B just lingering right outside my door. He made some excuse, muttered something and pretended he was looking through his pockets for his mail key, but you don't stand there in dead silence for five minutes looking for a key. And ever since that specific day, it’s just been constant. A year and a month of them watching when I take my trash out, watching when I check the mail, listening through the drywall. \n\nI know they’re reporting everything back to the office. The office probably wants to find a reason to kick me out so they can put down some cheap laminate flooring and charge double the rent to some younger folks. That's how these places work, I've seen it happen. So they have the neighbors doing their dirty work, keeping tabs on me, slipping their little reports to the manager. It’s exhausting, it really is, dealing with this for over a year. You’d think they would get bored of watching a tired old man sit on his couch, but no, thirteen months of this nonsense and they're still at it, day and night.\n\nDoctor: Have you lost interest in things you used to enjoy?\n\nPatient: Lost interest? Yeah, I'd say so. I'd say I've lost interest in just about everything, honestly. It's funny you ask that, because I was just thinking the other day about how different my Sundays used to be. I used to have a whole routine, you know? A whole schedule. I used to really look forward to choir practice. I'm not the best singer in the world, mind you, but I liked being part of it, the harmony, all those voices coming together. And then after choir, there was bridge. We had a regular group, four of us, and we'd play for hours. We weren't playing for money or anything, just bragging rights, but it was... it was nice. It felt good to use my brain like that, strategizing, trying to figure out what cards the others were holding. \n\nAnd cooking, too. I used to love making this big pot of beans every Sunday. My grandmother's recipe, with the ham hock and the onions, letting it simmer all day so the whole apartment smelled like it. I'd make enough to last me half the week. Well, see, the thing about that is... you've got it a little backwards, doc. If you're asking if they ever took a break from watching me, the answer is absolutely not. They never stopped. Not for one single day, not for a weekend, not for a holiday.

I actually thought to myself, well, maybe I'm finally catching a break from feeling so utterly miserable. 

But here's the kicker. Even then, even when I was eating my sandwiches and waking up with a little more fight in me, I still knew exactly what was happening out in that hallway. I'd be sitting there at my little kitchen table, feeling a bit lighter, but I still believed—no, I knew for a fact—that the neighbors were out there watching my door. I could feel them doing it. I knew they were still keeping their logs, still reporting every little noise I made right back to the management office. 

So, I might have had a few weeks where the depression backed off just a tiny bit and let me breathe, but the watching? The reporting? That never stopped. Not for a second. Even when I was feeling a little better, I was still a target to them. They just don't ever quit.

I know they're writing things down about exactly when I leave for the store and when I come back, and it's just... it's exhausting, honestly, having to look over your shoulder every single time you just want to step outside to check the mail.\n\nDoctor: Have you been hearing voices when no one is there?\n\nPatient: Voices? You know how these apartment buildings are, especially the older ones like mine. No, no, I wouldn't say that. I mean, I can talk just fine when I need to. Well, when there's actually someone to talk to, which isn't often these days, what with me staying inside all the time. Doc, I feel like we're going in circles a little bit here. Like I was just saying a minute ago with the whole sandwich thing... you're asking if it was exactly a full month now. 

See, the thing is, when you don't have a job to go to—which I haven't for a good long while now, just living on what I can get by on—and you're just sitting in the exact same apartment day in and day out, the days just sort of bleed into one another. So, if you're pinning me down and asking if it was exactly thirty days, a whole calendar month... I can't swear to it on a stack of Bibles. What I do know, like I was just trying to explain, is that there was definitely a spell of several weeks. Could have been three weeks, could have been five, I really couldn't tell you the exact math on it. But for those several weeks, I was eating a bit better, making those real meals instead of eating stale crackers, and I wasn't waking up feeling so completely hopeless and weighed down by everything. 

But as for the rest of it? The spying? That never stopped. Not for a day, let alone a month. Even when that heavy sadness lifted for those several weeks, I still believed—I knew for an absolute fact—that the neighbors were watching my door and reporting on me. I'd be chewing my food, feeling alright for once, but my eyes were still locked on that hallway. So, several weeks, yes, absolutely. But I couldn't tell you if it crossed the finish line into a full month. All I know is the mood got better for a spell, but the neighbors never quit.

Doc, I... I feel like we're just spinning our wheels here, going over the exact same ground we just covered. Didn't you just ask me this? I could swear you just asked me this exact same thing about five minutes ago. 

Look, I'll tell you again, just like I said before. I could actually breathe a little easier. \n\nBut—and this is the thing you really gotta understand—even during those few weeks when that heavy feeling took a little vacation, I still believed... well, I didn't just believe, I knew for a fact... that the neighbors were watching my door. I'd be sitting there at my little table, chewing my sandwich, feeling alright for a change, but my eyes would be glued to the crack under the front door. Because I knew they were out in that hallway. I knew they were still keeping their little logs and reporting every little thing I did to the building manager. \n\nThe sadness might have given me a break for those several weeks, sure. I wasn't waking up with that terrible dread. But those people? They never gave me a break. So, yes, to answer your question, there was a period of a few weeks where I wasn't feeling so down, but I absolutely still knew they were watching and reporting on me the whole time.\n\nDoctor: Aside from feeling depressed, have you had a long period where it was hard to speak much or show emotion, even when talking with other people?\n\nPatient: No, no, I wouldn't say that. It was all pouring out of me. \n\nSo, no, I've never had a time where I couldn't speak or show emotion. Once I get going, especially if I'm upset about something, like those notices on my door or the way the neighbors are always lurking around, I can get pretty worked up. My voice gets loud, my hands start shaking, I can feel my heart just hammering away in my chest. You can definitely tell exactly how I'm feeling when that happens. There's no hiding it. \n\nI remember this one time, oh, it must have been a few months back, right before that little spell where I was eating better. I had to call the management office because they’d left another one of those vague, threatening notes slipped under my door. I was so angry, so just... fed up with the whole situation, that I was practically shouting into the phone. The lady on the other end kept telling me to calm down, but I couldn't. I was pacing the floor, waving my arms around like a madman, even though she couldn't see me. I was just so full of emotion, you know? It was all pouring out of me. \n\nSo, no, I've never had a time where I couldn't speak or show emotion. If I'm feeling something, whether it's that heavy, gray sadness or that hot, burning anger about being spied on, it shows. It definitely shows. Sometimes I wish I could just turn it off, just be blank and not feel anything at all, but that's just not how I'm wired, I guess. The feelings are always right there, right on the surface, ready to spill over the second I open my mouth.\n\nDoctor: Was there ever a full month when you still knew your neighbors were watching and reporting on you, but you were not feeling depressed?\n\nPatient: Doc, I feel like we're going in circles a little bit here. Like I was just saying a minute ago with the whole sandwich thing... you're asking if it was exactly a full month now. \n\nSee, the thing is, when you don't have a job to go to—which I haven't for a good long while now, just living on what I can get by on—and you're just sitting in the exact same apartment day in and day out, the days just sort of bleed into one another. Monday feels like Thursday, Sunday feels like Tuesday. You lose track of the calendar when there's nowhere you have to be. \n\nSo, if you're pinning me down and asking if it was exactly thirty days, a whole calendar month... I can't swear to it on a stack of Bibles. What I do know, like I was just trying to explain, is that there was definitely a spell of several weeks. Could have been three weeks, could have been five, I really couldn't tell you the exact math on it. But for those several weeks, I was eating a bit better, making those real meals instead of eating stale crackers, and I wasn't waking up feeling so completely hopeless and weighed down by everything. \n\nBut as for the rest of it? The spying? That never stopped. Not for a day, let alone a month. Even when that heavy sadness lifted for those several weeks, I still believed—I knew for an absolute fact—that the neighbors were watching my door and reporting on me. I'd be chewing my food, feeling alright for once, but my eyes were still locked on that hallway. So, several weeks, yes, absolutely. But I couldn't tell you if it crossed the finish line into a full month. All I know is the mood got better for a spell, but the neighbors never quit.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever felt that ordinary things around you—like TV shows, radio, or strangers’ comments—were sending special messages meant specifically for you?\n\nPatient: No, no, nothing like that. I mean, I watch TV, sure. Mostly the old reruns, you know? The stuff from the seventies and eighties, back when things made a little more sense. The comedies, mostly. M*A*S*H, Barney Miller, that sort of thing. I'll just leave it on in the background while I'm sitting at the table, just to have some noise in the apartment so it's not so dead quiet all the time. But it's just a TV show. Hawkeye Pierce isn't trying to talk to me through the screen, if that's what you're asking. \n\nAnd the radio... well, I don't really listen to the radio much anymore. Used to, back when I had a car, I'd listen to the classic rock stations, maybe a little talk radio if the music was no good. But in the apartment, it's just the TV. And strangers? Like I said, I don't go out much. I stay inside. No, they're just... they're just boxes making noise. They don't know who I am, and they certainly aren't trying to send me any secret codes or anything crazy like that. I'm just a guy sitting in his apartment, trying to get by, trying to keep an eye on the door. That's all.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever seen something that other people could not see?\n\nPatient: See things? Like... like visions or something? No, no, definitely not. I actually had to go down to the pharmacy a couple years back and buy one of those cheap pairs of reading glasses off the little spinning rack they have near the register. Just the plastic ones, you know? Because I was having trouble making out the small print on the back of the soup cans and the cracker boxes. Sometimes I'll sit there in the armchair for... oh, it feels like hours, just staring at that little gap between the bottom of the door and the linoleum, just waiting for the shadow to shift. But that's a real shadow, from a real person who's actually out there spying on me. It's not some trick of the light or my mind playing games with me. \n\nSo, no, besides just needing those cheap glasses to read, my eyes only show me what's really in the room with me. Just the old furniture, the TV, and the door. Always the door. I've never seen anything that someone else wouldn't see if they were sitting right there next to me.\n\nDoctor: Was there ever a full month when you still believed your neighbors were watching and reporting on you, but you were not feeling depressed?\n\nPatient: Doc, I... I mean, my eyes aren't exactly what they used to be, I'll give you that. I'm fifty-nine now, and... well, things get a little fuzzy around the edges sometimes. I actually had to go down to the pharmacy a couple years back and buy one of those cheap pairs of reading glasses off the little spinning rack they have near the register. Just the plastic ones, you know? Because I was having trouble making out the small print on the back of the soup cans and the cracker boxes. And, of course, I have to put them on to read those damn notes the neighbors keep sliding under my door. \n\nBut as far as seeing things that aren't actually there, like... I don't know, ghosts or imaginary people? No, never anything like that. If I see it, it's really there. Like the shadows under the door crack. When they're standing out there in the hall, just waiting and listening, I can see their shadow blocking the light from the hallway. I see that plain as day. Sometimes I'll sit there in the armchair for... oh, it feels like hours, just staring at that little gap between the bottom of the door and the linoleum, just waiting for the shadow to shift. But that's a real shadow, from a real person who's actually out there spying on me. It's not some trick of the light or my mind playing games with me. \n\nSo, no, besides just needing those cheap glasses to read, my eyes only show me what's really in the room with me. Just the old furniture, the TV, and the door. Always the door. I've never seen anything that someone else wouldn't see if they were sitting right there next to me.\n\nDoctor: Was there ever a full month when you still believed your neighbors were watching and reporting on you, but you were not feeling depressed?\n\nPatient: Doc, I... I feel like we're just spinning our wheels here, going over the exact same ground we just covered. Didn't you just ask me this? I could swear you just asked me this exact same thing about five minutes ago. \n\nLook, I'll tell you again, just like I said before. When you're cooped up in the same apartment, day after day, week after week, and you don't have a job to go to, you don't have anywhere you're supposed to be at nine in the morning... time just sort of loses its meaning, you know? It gets all stretched out and blurry. So if you're asking me to swear on a stack of Bibles that it was exactly thirty days, exactly one full calendar month, I just can't do that. I don't have that kind of a calendar in my head anymore.\n\nBut what I *can* tell you, what I know for a fact, is that there was definitely a spell... a period of several weeks in there. Might have been three weeks, might have been five, I don't know the exact math. But for those several weeks, the heavy stuff lifted a bit. I was actually eating real food, making myself something decent instead of just chewing on those stale saltines I keep in the cupboard. And I wasn't waking up with that... that crushing weight on my chest, feeling so completely hopeless about everything. The mood definitely got better for a spell.\n\nBut the neighbors? The watching and the reporting? That never stopped. Not for a single second. Even when I was feeling a bit lighter, even when I was actually managing to eat a decent meal, I still knew—I knew for an absolute fact—that they were right out there in the hall. I'd be sitting there, chewing my food, feeling alright for once, but my eyes were still locked dead on that door. I knew they were watching, I knew they were writing things down. So, yes, several weeks where I felt better, absolutely. But I still believed they were out there the whole time. I just can't tell you if it crossed the finish line into exactly a full month.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone told you that your speech or behavior became very disorganized or hard to follow?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, people don't talk to me much these days, mostly because I don't give them the chance. But... well, yeah, I guess there have been a few times. The guy at the corner store, for one. I went down there a while back, maybe a couple months ago, just to get some milk and maybe a loaf of bread, you know, the basics. And I was trying to explain to him why I needed him to double-bag the groceries, because I didn't want the bottoms falling out on the stairs, and somehow I got to talking about the rent. \n\nBecause the rent, you see, they raised it again, and it's just getting impossible on what I have coming in. I was telling the clerk about the marina, and the boats, and then... well, I don't know how I got there, but I started talking about choir robes. My aunt used to sing in a choir, had these big heavy maroon robes, and I was trying to explain how the fabric felt, because it reminded me of something, maybe the curtains in the apartment. \n\nAnd then, of course, I had to mention the wires in the walls, because that's the real problem, isn't it? The wires they use to listen in. I was trying to explain how the wires connect everything, how they run right behind the plaster where you can't see them but you know they're there. And I'm trying to lay it all out for him, making the connections—the rent, the marina, the robes, the wires—and he just... he just stared at me. He had this look on his face, like his eyes were glazed over, and he said, \"Buddy, I don't know what you're talking about, just take your groceries.\" \n\nHe looked at me like I'd skipped half the story, like I was speaking Greek or something. But to me, it all made perfect sense, it all connected right up. I was just trying to give him the full picture. But I guess... I guess maybe it didn't come out the way it sounded in my head. So, yeah, I suppose people have looked at me like I'm not making sense, but they just aren't following the threads, you know? They don't see how it all ties together.\n\nDoctor: Have there been times when your thoughts felt jumbled or hard for you to keep in order?\n\nPatient: Jumbled... yeah. Yeah, you could definitely say that. It's like... well, if you were to walk into my kitchen right now, you'd see this whole mess on the corner of my table. It's just this big, messy pile of bills and appointment cards. They just keep piling up, week after week. I try to stay on top of it, I really do. I'll pull out that wobbly old wooden chair, sit myself down, put on those cheap reading glasses I was telling you about, and I'll pick up the top piece of mail. \n\nBut then... I don't know, it's like my brain just completely stalls out on me. I'll look at the paper, and I'll read the exact same line, over and over and over again. 'Please remit payment by...' or 'Your upcoming appointment is...' I read the words, and I know they're English, but they just don't mean anything. They don't stick together in my head. It's like wading through thick mud. \n\nAnd then I'll have a bill in one hand, and maybe a clinic card in the other, and I just stare at them because I completely lose the ability to figure out what to do. Do I need to find a stamp? \n\nMy thoughts just get all tangled up, like a bird's nest of old fishing line. I'll sit there for twenty, thirty minutes, just reading that exact same sentence about the balance due, trying to force my brain to make a simple decision, but it just won't go. The gears won't turn. So I end up putting it all right back down in the pile and walking away. It's just... it's exhausting, you know? Trying to force your thoughts into a straight line when they just want to scatter everywhere. So the pile just sits there, getting bigger, because I can't keep my head straight enough to sort it out.\n\nDoctor: For at least six months, have you been having these experiences of your neighbors watching you and reporting on you?\n\nPatient: Six months? I walked in, and the way the woman at the desk looked at me... and then the way my next-door neighbor just happened to be walking out of the office at the exact same time, giving her this little nod... it all just clicked. I saw the whole picture right then and there. \n\nSince that day\n\nDoctor: Was there ever a full month when you still knew your neighbors were watching and reporting on you, but you were not feeling depressed?\n\nPatient: A full month? It was a stretch of time where things felt just a little bit different in my head. \n\nI remember it because I was actually eating a bit better. Usually, I don't have much of an appetite for anything, just sort of pick at stale crackers or whatever's sitting on the counter, but during those few weeks, I had actually gone down and bought a big carton of eggs and some of that oatmeal with the apples and cinnamon. I was getting up and actually boiling the water, making a real breakfast. And I wasn't waking up feeling so... so heavy, you know? Usually, I open my eyes and there's just this crushing hopelessness right on my chest, this feeling like there's absolutely no point in putting my feet on the floor. I could swear you just asked me this exact same thing about five minutes ago. \n\nLook, I'll tell you again, just like I said before. When you're cooped up in the same apartment, day after day, week after week, and you don't have a job to go to, you don't have anywhere you're supposed to be at nine in the morning... time just sort of loses its meaning, you know? It gets all stretched out and blurry. So if you're asking me to swear on a stack of Bibles that it was exactly thirty days, exactly one full calendar month, I just can't do that. I don't have that kind of a calendar in my head anymore.\n\nBut what I *can* tell you, what I know for a fact, is that there was definitely a spell... a period of several weeks in there. I was actually eating real food, making myself something decent instead of just chewing on those stale saltines I keep in the cupboard. The watching and the reporting? That never stopped. Not for a single second. Even when I was feeling a bit lighter, even when I was actually managing to eat a decent meal, I still knew—I knew for an absolute fact—that they were right out there in the hall. I'd be sitting there, chewing my food, feeling alright for once, but my eyes were still locked dead on that door. I knew they were watching, I knew they were writing things down. I went down there a while back, maybe a couple months ago, just to get some milk and maybe a loaf of bread, you know, the basics. I was telling the clerk about the marina, and the boats, and then... well, I don't know how I got there, but I started talking about choir robes. My aunt used to sing in a choir, had these big heavy maroon robes, and I was trying to explain how the fabric felt, because it reminded me of something, maybe the curtains in the apartment. \n\nAnd then, of course, I had to mention the wires in the walls, because that's the real problem, isn't it? But it's just a TV show. Hawkeye Pierce isn't trying to talk to me through the screen, if that's what you're asking. \n\nAnd the radio... well, I don't really listen to the radio much anymore. Used to, back when I had a car, I'd listen to the classic rock stations, maybe a little talk radio if the music was no good. But in the apartment, it's just the TV. And strangers? Like I said, I don't go out much. I stay inside. So there aren't any strangers around to make comments, special messages or otherwise. \n\nThe only people sending messages are the neighbors, and they aren't using the TV to do it. They're just writing down everything I do and slipping those vague little notes under my door. That's real. That's actually happening right outside my living room. But the TV? The radio? No, they're just... they're just boxes making noise. They don't know who I am, and they certainly aren't trying to send me any secret codes or anything crazy like that. I'm just a guy sitting in his apartment, trying to get by, trying to keep an eye on the door. That's all.\n\nDoctor: Have you ever seen something that other people could not see?\n\nPatient: See things? Like... like visions or something? No, no, definitely not. I mean, my eyes aren't exactly what they used to be, I'll give you that. I'm fifty-nine now, and... well, things get a little fuzzy around the edges sometimes. I actually had to go down to the pharmacy a couple years back and buy one of those cheap pairs of reading glasses off the little spinning rack they have near the register. Just the plastic ones, you know? Because I was having trouble making out the small print on the back of the soup cans and the cracker boxes. And, of course, I have to put them on to read those damn notes the neighbors keep sliding under my door. \n\nBut as far as seeing things that aren't actually there, like... I don't know, ghosts or imaginary people? No, never anything like that. If I see it, it's really there. Like the shadows under the door crack. When they're standing out there in the hall, just waiting and listening, I can see their shadow blocking the light from the hallway. I see that plain as day. Sometimes I'll sit there in the armchair for... oh, it feels like hours, just staring at that little gap between the bottom of the door and the linoleum, just waiting for the shadow to shift. But that's a real shadow, from a real person who's actually out there spying on me. It's not some trick of the light or my mind playing games with me. \n\nSo, no, besides just needing those cheap glasses to read, my eyes only show me what's really in the room with me. Just the old furniture, the TV, and the door. Always the door. I've never seen anything that someone else wouldn't see if they were sitting right there next to me.\n\nDoctor: Was there ever a full month when you still believed your neighbors were watching and reporting on you, but you were not feeling depressed?\n\nPatient: Doc, I... I feel like we're just spinning our wheels here, going over the exact same ground we just covered. Didn't you just ask me this? I could swear you just asked me this exact same thing about five minutes ago. \n\nLook, I'll tell you again, just like I said before. When you're cooped up in the same apartment, day after day, week after week, and you don't have a job to go to, you don't have anywhere you're supposed to be at nine in the morning... time just sort of loses its meaning, you know? It gets all stretched out and blurry. So if you're asking me to swear on a stack of Bibles that it was exactly thirty days, exactly one full calendar month, I just can't do that. I don't have that kind of a calendar in my head anymore.\n\nBut what I *can* tell you, what I know for a fact, is that there was definitely a spell... a period of several weeks in there. Might have been three weeks, might have been five, I don't know the exact math. But for those several weeks, the heavy stuff lifted a bit. I was actually eating real food, making myself something decent instead of just chewing on those stale saltines I keep in the cupboard. And I wasn't waking up with that... that crushing weight on my chest, feeling so completely hopeless about everything. The mood definitely got better for a spell.\n\nBut the neighbors? The watching and the reporting? That never stopped. Not for a single second. Even when I was feeling a bit lighter, even when I was actually managing to eat a decent meal, I still knew—I knew for an absolute fact—that they were right out there in the hall. I'd be sitting there, chewing my food, feeling alright for once, but my eyes were still locked dead on that door. I knew they were watching, I knew they were writing things down. So, yes, several weeks where I felt better, absolutely. But I still believed they were out there the whole time. I just can't tell you if it crossed the finish line into exactly a full month.\n\nDoctor: Has anyone told you that your speech or behavior became very disorganized or hard to follow?\n\nPatient: Well, I mean, people don't talk to me much these days, mostly because I don't give them the chance. But... well, yeah, I guess there have been a few times. The guy at the corner store, for one. I went down there a while back, maybe a couple months ago, just to get some milk and maybe a loaf of bread, you know, the basics. And I was trying to explain to him why I needed him to double-bag the groceries, because I didn't want the bottoms falling out on the stairs, and somehow I got to talking about the rent. \n\nBecause the rent, you see, they raised it again, and it's just getting impossible on what I have coming in. So I'm talking about the rent, and then I remembered this time back when I used to go down to the marina, just to watch the boats, back before things got so bad. I was telling the clerk about the marina, and the boats, and then... well, I don't know how I got there, but I started talking about choir robes. My aunt used to sing in a choir, had these big heavy maroon robes, and I was trying to explain how the fabric felt, because it reminded me of something, maybe the curtains in the apartment. \n\nAnd then, of course, I had to mention the wires in the walls, because that's the real problem, isn't it? The wires they use to listen in. I was trying to explain how the wires connect everything, how they run right behind the plaster where you can't see them but you know they're there. And I'm trying to lay it all out for him, making the connections—the rent, the marina, the robes, the wires—and he just... he just stared at me. He had this look on his face, like his eyes were glazed over, and he said, \"Buddy, I don't know what you're talking about, just take your groceries.\" \n\nHe looked at me like I'd skipped half the story, like I was speaking Greek or something. But to me, it all made perfect sense, it all connected right up. I was just trying to give him the full picture. But I guess... I guess maybe it didn't come out the way it sounded in my head. So, yeah, I suppose people have looked at me like I'm not making sense, but they just aren't following the threads, you know? They don't see how it all ties together.\n\nDoctor: Have there been times when your thoughts felt jumbled or hard for you to keep in order?\n\nPatient: Jumbled... yeah. Yeah, you could definitely say that. It's like... well, if you were to walk into my kitchen right now, you'd see this whole mess on the corner of my table. It's just this big, messy pile of bills and appointment cards. They just keep piling up, week after week. I try to stay on top of it, I really do. I'll pull out that wobbly old wooden chair, sit myself down, put on those cheap reading glasses I was telling you about, and I'll pick up the top piece of mail. \n\nBut then... I don't know, it's like my brain just completely stalls out on me. I'll look at the paper, and I'll read the exact same line, over and over and over again. 'Please remit payment by...' or 'Your upcoming appointment is...' I read the words, and I know they're English, but they just don't mean anything. They don't stick together in my head. It's like wading through thick mud. \n\nAnd then I'll have a bill in one hand, and maybe a clinic card in the other, and I just stare at them because I completely lose the ability to figure out what to do. I just can't decide what needs doing first. Which one is more important? Do I pay this? Do I call them? Do I need to find a stamp? \n\nMy thoughts just get all tangled up, like a bird's nest of old fishing line. I'll sit there for twenty, thirty minutes, just reading that exact same sentence about the balance due, trying to force my brain to make a simple decision, but it just won't go. The gears won't turn. So I end up putting it all right back down in the pile and walking away. It's just... it's exhausting, you know? Trying to force your thoughts into a straight line when they just want to scatter everywhere. So the pile just sits there, getting bigger, because I can't keep my head straight enough to sort it out.\n\nDoctor: For at least six months, have you been having these experiences of your neighbors watching you and reporting on you?\n\nPatient: Six months? Doc, if it had only been six months, I might still be able to get a decent night's sleep every now and then. No, we... we passed the six-month mark a long, long time ago. It's funny you say six months, because that would mean it started in the summer, but it didn't. I know for an absolute fact it didn't start in the summer, because I remember having to put my heavy winter coat on when I first realized what they were all doing. \n\nIt's been... well, let's see. It's been a year, easily. Actually, more than that. A year and a month. Yeah, about thirteen months of this. And the thing is, it's not just the folks living on my floor, either. It's the apartment office, too. The management office downstairs, the people who collect the rent. They're all in on it together, the neighbors and the office. \n\nI started putting the pieces together a year and a month ago, right around the time I had to go down there to drop off some paperwork. I walked in, and the way the woman at the desk looked at me... and then the way my next-door neighbor just happened to be walking out of the office at the exact same time, giving her this little nod... it all just clicked. I saw the whole picture right then and there. \n\nSince that day\n\nDoctor: Was there ever a full month when you still knew your neighbors were watching and reporting on you, but you were not feeling depressed?\n\nPatient: A full month? Well, I don't know if I'd say it was exactly a whole thirty days on the calendar, you know, marking off the boxes, but... there was definitely a spell of several weeks in there. It was a stretch of time where things felt just a little bit different in my head. \n\nI remember it because I was actually eating a bit better. Usually, I don't have much of an appetite for anything, just sort of pick at stale crackers or whatever's sitting on the counter, but during those few weeks, I had actually gone down and bought a big carton of eggs and some of that oatmeal with the apples and cinnamon. I was getting up and actually boiling the water, making a real breakfast. And I wasn't waking up feeling so... so heavy, you know? Usually, I open my eyes and there's just this crushing hopelessness right on my chest, this feeling like there's absolutely no point in putting my feet on the floor. But for those several weeks, that dark cloud sort of lifted a bit. I'd wake up and think, 'Alright, I can get up today. I can make my oatmeal.' \n\nBut... and this is the important part, Doc, this is what you have to understand... even though I was feeling a bit lighter, even though I wasn't dragging myself through the mud every morning, the reality of what was going on out in the hallway didn't change one bit. I'd be standing there at my stove, feeling decent for a change, eating a hot meal, but I still knew they were out there. I still believed—well, I didn't just believe it, I knew it—that the neighbors were watching my door. I'd still keep the kitchen light off so they couldn't see my shadow under the doorframe. I could still hear the floorboards creaking out there when they'd stop by my door to listen in and take their notes to report back to the management office. \n\nSo, yeah, my mood was better, and I wasn't waking up wanting to just disappear into the mattress for a few weeks there, but the watching... the watching and the reporting, that never took a day off. They were still right there, keeping tabs on me, same as always.\n\nDoctor: At any point during this past year, did your depressed mood stay away for a full month while you still believed your neighbors were watching and reporting on you?\n\nPatient: Well, like I was just saying... it's hard to say if it was exactly thirty days, you know, a full calendar month, but... yeah, there was that stretch. That spell of several weeks where the heavy, dark feeling in my chest wasn't there. I wasn't waking up feeling so completely hopeless, like I was just a ghost haunting my own bed. \n\nI remember it so clearly because, like I mentioned, I was eating better. I was making that oatmeal. I'd stand there in the kitchen, actually feeling okay, not wanting to just cry or stare at the wall. I felt... normal, almost. Or as normal as I get these days. \n\nBut the thing is, Doc, and I really need you to hear me on this... my mood being better didn't change the facts of what was happening outside my apartment. Not one bit. I'd be stirring my oatmeal, feeling fine, but I still knew—I still absolutely believed, because it was true—that they were out there. I'd still keep the lights low. I'd still listen for the floorboards creaking. I knew the neighbors were still watching my door, still taking their little notes, still reporting back to the office. \n\nSo, yes, the depression lifted for those several weeks, but the watching... the watching never stopped. Not for a single day. They were always there, even when I was feeling better.\n\nDoctor: During this past year, was there a time when your depressed mood was completely gone for a full month?\n\nPatient: No, no, not a full month. I mean, I know I just went on about that stretch where I was making the oatmeal and feeling a bit lighter, but if we're talking about the whole year... the whole thirteen months since I really started putting the pieces together... no, the depression hasn't ever stayed gone for a whole thirty days straight. \n\nI mean, if you look at the big picture, the grand scheme of things since I moved into that place... for the vast majority of the time, I've just been so incredibly low. Even on the days where my head felt a little clearer, where the fog pulled back just a tiny bit and I could string a thought together without it feeling like lifting a boulder... even on those days, that heavy, useless feeling was still right there under the surface. It's like... it's like a stain that won't wash out, you know? \n\nMost days, I just feel completely useless. Like I'm taking up space. I don't have any interest in the things I used to do. I used to like tinkering with radios, you know, taking them apart and fixing the antennas, but I haven't touched my tools in... well, I can't even remember the last time. The tools are just sitting in the bottom of the closet, gathering dust. I look at them and I just feel tired. So, yeah, even when I had that brief spell of feeling okay, the reality is that for most of this past year, most of the time since I've been in that apartment, I've been dragging around this awful, low feeling, just completely uninterested in everything and feeling like I don't matter at all."
